params.question: Under the PCPNDT Act, what determines whether performing a prenatal diagnostic technique such as ultrasound is lawful or criminal?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Act does not distinguish by equipment type. Ultrasound, amniocentesis, and genetic tests are all lawful when used for medical diagnosis — it is the purpose, not the instrument, that matters.

answers.text: The gestational age at which the test is performed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no trimester-based exemption. The prohibition on sex determination applies at every gestational age throughout pregnancy.

answers.text: The purpose for which the technique is used

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The same technique is lawful when used to detect chromosomal, genetic, or congenital abnormalities, but criminal when used to determine or disclose foetal sex. Purpose is the dividing line.

answers.text: Whether the pregnant woman has given written consent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Consent does not legalise sex determination. The prohibition is absolute — it applies regardless of the woman's wishes, consent, or stated intentions.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is that purpose determines legality. The same ultrasound that lawfully detects congenital anomalies becomes criminal when used to determine or disclose foetal sex.
Exactly right. The PCPNDT Act targets the misuse of prenatal techniques, not the techniques themselves. Detecting disease is lawful; identifying sex for selection is criminal.

interactions.label: Under the PCPNDT Act, the prescribed Form F must be completed for every pregnant

params.question: Under the PCPNDT Act, the prescribed Form F must be completed for every pregnant woman undergoing a prenatal diagnostic test. What does this form include?

answers.text: A signed declaration that the sex of the foetus was not detected or disclosed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Form F records the woman's particulars, the clinical indication for the test, and crucially a signed declaration that foetal sex was neither determined nor revealed. An incomplete Form F is itself a prosecutable offence — one of the most common grounds for action.

answers.text: The radiologist's detailed interpretation of all ultrasound findings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A detailed radiology report is standard clinical practice but is separate from Form F. Form F is a statutory compliance document specific to the PCPNDT Act, not an imaging report.

answers.text: Written consent from the pregnant woman's spouse or next of kin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Act does not require spousal or family consent in Form F. It requires documentation of the patient's details, the medical indication, and a declaration regarding sex non-disclosure.

answers.text: The manufacturer's calibration certificate for the ultrasound machine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Equipment records are tracked separately — manufacturers must report sales to the Appropriate Authority. Form F pertains to each patient encounter, not to equipment maintenance.

overallFeedback.feedback: Form F is the statutory document that records patient particulars, the clinical indication, and a signed declaration that foetal sex was not determined or disclosed. Its incompleteness is the most common ground for prosecution under the Act.
Well done. Form F is the Act's most important day-to-day compliance document. Keeping it complete and accurate for every patient is a legal obligation — failure is itself a criminal offence.

params.question: After a routine anomaly scan, a family assures you they will not terminate the pregnancy and asks you to 'just hint' at the baby's sex. What is the correct course of action?

answers.text: Disclose the sex since the family has confirmed no termination is planned

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The family's stated intent is legally irrelevant under the PCPNDT Act. The prohibition on sex disclosure is absolute — it applies regardless of any assurance the family gives.

answers.text: Provide an indirect or coded response so there is no explicit disclosure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A hint, gesture, or coded phrase counts as disclosure under the Act. Indirect communication of foetal sex is equally a criminal offence — the law specifically covers this.

answers.text: Refuse clearly, explain the legal prohibition, and document the refusal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Refuse compassionately but firmly, explain that the PCPNDT Act binds you personally with criminal penalties including imprisonment and loss of registration, and record the interaction. The anomaly scan itself remains entirely proper.

answers.text: Refer the family to the facility's senior radiologist for a decision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The prohibition binds every medical professional individually. Referring the request to a senior colleague does not discharge your legal responsibility — it may in fact implicate both of you.

overallFeedback.feedback: The PCPNDT Act requires you to refuse any request for sex disclosure — directly or indirectly — regardless of the family's stated intentions. Refuse clearly, explain why, and document the refusal.
Exactly right. A clear refusal, a brief explanation of the law's purpose, and documentation protect both the patient and you. Remember: the scan is lawful — only sex disclosure is forbidden.
